ety.text: From Middle English luk, lukke, from Middle Dutch luc, geluc, gelucke (“good luck, fortune”) or Middle Low German lücke, gelücke (“lot, fortune, fate, luck”), of obscure origin; perhaps ultimately related to German Lücke (“gap, opening”) in the sense of "space or opportunity", hence "chance".

senses.d: Something that happens to someone by chance, a chance occurrence.
ex: The raffle is just a matter of luck.
Gilbert had some bad luck yesterday — he got pick-pocketed and lost fifty dollars.
Sometimes it takes a bit of luck to get success.
I couldn't believe my luck when I found a fifty dollar bill on the street.

senses.d: A superstitious feeling that brings fortune or success.
ex: He blew on the dice for luck.
I wish you lots of luck for the exam tomorrow.
I tried for ages to find a pair of blue suede shoes, but didn't have any luck.
He has a lot of luck with the ladies. Perhaps it's because of his new motorbike.

senses.d: The results of a random number generator.
ex: The creators of tool-assisted speedruns often manipulate luck to get the most favorable results in order to save the most time.

senses.d: To find something through good fortune; used with into, on, onto or upon.
ex: I lucked upon a seat, settled in, nodded off and 20 minutes later heard my name being called by the admitting nurse.

grp.label: something that happens to someone by chance

ety.text: From Old French cheance (“accident, chance, luck”), inherited from Vulgar Latin *cadentia (“falling”). Doublet of cadence, a borrowing from Italian.
